nameStory: The barrelfish gets its name from its deep, rounded body shape that resembles a barrel when viewed from the side. This stocky, cylindrical build helps it navigate the crushing pressures of the deep ocean where it makes its home.
description: The barrelfish is a deep-water ocean fish that lives far below the surface in the cold, dark depths of the North Atlantic. It has a robust, barrel-shaped body that's built for life in the deep sea where water pressure is immense. These fish are rarely seen by casual observers since they live in deep waters far from shore, making any sighting in New England waters quite special.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, rounded, barrel-like body that feels solid and muscular when handled, with a compressed profile that's taller than it is wide

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found only in deep ocean waters far from shore, typically brought up by deep-sea fishing or occasionally washing ashore

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Continuous dorsal fin running along most of the back, with well-developed pectoral fins suited for maneuvering in deep water

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized deep-water fish, noticeably hefty and solid-feeling for its length due to the barrel-shaped build

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark coloration typical of deep-sea fish, appearing blackish or dark brown with a somewhat metallic sheen when fresh

habitat: Barrelfish live in the deep, open ocean waters of the North Atlantic, far from New England's coastline. They inhabit the bathypelagic zone - the deep, dark waters where sunlight never reaches and pressure is extreme. Any barrelfish found in New England would likely be a very rare deep-sea fishing catch or an unusual specimen that has washed ashore.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare sightings possible from deep-sea fishing expeditions as fishing activity increases with improving weather conditions.
seasonality.summer: Peak deep-sea fishing season offers the best chance for encounters, though sightings remain exceptionally uncommon in New England waters.
seasonality.fall: Continued deep-water fishing activity may occasionally bring specimens to surface, but encounters remain very rare.
seasonality.winter: Minimal chance of observation due to reduced deep-sea fishing activity and harsh ocean conditions limiting access to deep waters.

funFact: Unlike most fish in the medusafish family, barrelfish completely ignore jellyfish and never seek shelter under their bells - they're the independent loners of their family, preferring the solitary life in the deep ocean depths!
confusionNotes: With only 2 recorded observations in New England, barrelfish are so rare that confusion with other species is unlikely - if you think you've found one, you're probably looking at a more common deep-water species or coastal fish instead.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "medusafish" (family Centrolophidae), barrelfish don't actually associate with jellyfish like many of their relatives do. This makes them somewhat unusual within their own family, as most medusafishes use jellyfish for protection or food.
compareHints: Barrelfish are the only species in their genus (Hyperoglyphe) found in New England waters, making them unique in the region. Compared to other medusafishes in the area, barrelfish are distinguished by their characteristic barrel shape and their lack of association with jellyfish. Their deep-bodied, robust build sets them apart from the more streamlined profiles of related species.
